{{Short description|Fourth-order PDE in continuum mechanics}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''biharmonic equation''' is a fourth-order [[partial differential equation]] which arises in areas of [[continuum mechanics]], including [[linear elasticity]] theory and the solution of [[Stokes flow]]s. Specifically, it is used in the modeling of thin structures that react [[Elasticity (physics)|elastically]] to external forces.

== Notation ==
It is written as
<math display="block">\nabla^4 \varphi = 0</math>
or
<math display="block">\nabla^2 \nabla^2 \varphi = 0</math>
or
<math display="block">\Delta^2 \varphi = 0</math>
where <math>\nabla^4</math>, which is the [[fourth power]] of the [[del]] operator and the square of the [[Laplacian]] operator <math>\nabla^2</math> (or <math>\Delta</math>), is known as the '''biharmonic operator''' or the '''bilaplacian operator'''.  In [[Cartesian coordinates]], it can be written in <math>n</math> dimensions as:
<math display="block">
\nabla^4 \varphi = \sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n \partial_i\partial_i\partial_j\partial_j \varphi
= \left(\sum_{i=1}^n \partial_i\partial_i\right) \left(\sum_{j=1}^n \partial_j\partial_j\right) \varphi.
</math>
Because the formula here contains a summation of indices, many mathematicians prefer the notation <math>\Delta^2</math> over <math>\nabla^4</math> because the former makes clear which of the indices of the four nabla operators are contracted over.

For example, in three dimensional [[Cartesian coordinates]] the biharmonic equation has the form
<math display="block">
{\partial^4 \varphi\over \partial x^4 } +
{\partial^4 \varphi\over \partial y^4 } +
{\partial^4 \varphi\over \partial z^4 } + 
2{\partial^4 \varphi\over \partial x^2\partial y^2} +
2{\partial^4 \varphi\over \partial y^2\partial z^2} +
2{\partial^4 \varphi\over \partial x^2\partial z^2} = 0.
</math>
As another example, in ''n''-dimensional [[real coordinate space]] without the origin <math>\left( \mathbb{R}^n \setminus \mathbf 0 \right) </math>,
<math display="block">\nabla^4 \left({1\over r}\right) = {3(15-8n+n^2)\over r^5}</math>
where
<math display="block">r = \sqrt{x_1^2 + x_2^2 +\cdots + x_n^2}.</math>
which shows, for ''n''=3 and ''n''=5 only, <math>\frac{1}{r}</math> is a solution to the biharmonic equation.

A solution to the biharmonic equation is called a '''biharmonic function'''. Any [[harmonic function]] is biharmonic, but the converse is not always true.

In two-dimensional [[polar coordinates]], the biharmonic equation is
<math display="block">
\frac{1}{r} \frac{\partial}{\partial r} \left(r \frac{\partial}{\partial r} \left(\frac{1}{r} \frac{\partial}{\partial r} \left(r \frac{\partial \varphi}{\partial r}\right) \right)\right)
 + \frac{2}{r^2} \frac{\partial^4 \varphi}{\partial \theta^2 \partial r^2}
 + \frac{1}{r^4} \frac{\partial^4 \varphi}{\partial \theta^4}
 - \frac{2}{r^3} \frac{\partial^3 \varphi}{\partial \theta^2 \partial r}
 + \frac{4}{r^4} \frac{\partial^2 \varphi}{\partial \theta^2} = 0
</math>
which can be solved by [[separation of variables]]. The result is the [[Michell solution]].

==2-dimensional space==
The general solution to the 2-dimensional case is
<math display="block">
x v(x,y) - y u(x,y) + w(x,y)
</math>
where <math>u(x,y)</math>, <math>v(x,y)</math> and <math>w(x,y)</math> are [[harmonic functions]] and <math>v(x,y)</math> is a  [[harmonic conjugate]] of <math>u(x,y)</math>.

Just as [[harmonic functions]] in 2 variables are closely related to complex [[analytic functions]], so are biharmonic functions in 2 variables. The general form of a biharmonic function in 2 variables can also be written as
<math display="block">
\operatorname{Im}(\bar{z}f(z) + g(z))
</math>
where <math>f(z)</math> and <math>g(z)</math> are [[analytic functions]].
